text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Monday.

GERMANY - Bund futures were solidly higher in late trade, maintaining gains posted in the morning linked to firm Treasuries and a technical correction to losses last week. The June Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 101.74, up 0.24 from Friday's settlement price.
BRITAIN - UK gilts clung fast to early gains and settled 12/32 high on the day. The June long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 111-28/32 up 12/32 from Friday's settlement price.

FRANCE - March bond futures traded in tight range after being marked higher at open. 130.98 support continues to hold after test late in session. The March notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 131.12 up 0.18 from Friday's settlement price.

ITALY - Italian debt markets failed to haul themselves out of a Monday morning depression in late business after speculation of a possible delay in EMU. The June bond future on LIFFE was trading at 127.25 down 0.35 from Friday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - U.S. Treasuries were narrowly mixed in soft late morning trade. Lack of fresh data sent players to sidelines. The June Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 110-06/32, up 03/32 from Friday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 6.82 percent.

JAPAN - The key June Japanese government bond (JGB) futures contract ended slightly higher in Tokyo on Monday, but off its earlier high. In after hours trading the March future on LIFFE was trading at 125.39, down 0.10 from Friday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

EUROBONDS - A quiet start to the week in the primary market saw the EBRD launch the longest Eurorand deal to date, a 30-year zero coupon offering. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development also set a two billion rand 20-year zero coupon deal to go with the five billion rand 30-year. Aggregate proceeds for the World Bank will just top $50 million. Toronto-Dominion lead managed. With no comparable South African government paper, dealers said investors were taking a gamble on the country's future. At full fees, the deals yielded around 14.5 percent at 20 years and 13.75 percent at 30 years.
